syllabus.clause: sift-up/sift-down, O(n) bottom-up build (sum-of-heights argument), heap as an implicit tree in an array.

at.step: A binary heap's tree lives entirely in one flat array — no pointers at all. A node at index i has its children at indices 2i+1 and 2i+2, and its parent at index floor((i−1)/2).
Sift-up: compare the new value with its parent; if the heap property already holds, stop. If not, swap them, and repeat from the new position.
Removing the minimum empties the root. Sift-down fills it: move the array's last element into the root, then walk it down, swapping with whichever child is smaller, until it's no longer out of order.

Building a heap from n arbitrary elements one insertion at a time costs O(n log n) — each of n insertions pays its own O(log n) sift-up. Sifting down from the bottom instead costs O(n): most nodes sit near the bottom, where a sift-down's own cost, bounded by that node's height, is small.

items.item: This topic's own measured swap counts (one-at-a-time versus bottom-up build) are scoped to its own examples.py input (n=4,000, decreasing order) and are not claimed to generalize exactly to every n or every input shape, only to the asymptotic bound each input shape is chosen to expose.

The implicit-array representation is what makes this topic's heap pointer-free: a node's own position in the array is the only state needed to compute both its parent and its children, with no stored links at all.

items.item: Heapify's linear-time build and heapsort's own sortdown phase are two separate mechanisms sharing one structure; this topic covers only the build, naming the sortdown phase only as where that build is actually used in production.

Insertion (sift-up) and extraction (sift-down) are each bounded by the tree's own height, not by n directly — the height bound is what makes a single operation O(log n), distinct from the separate claim about total build cost across n operations.
